samples.question: Somewhere in this picture there is one meter made of four separated tiles at the corners of a square, with plain background between them; every pale grey mark outside those four tiles is inert decoration. Three tiles are lamp banks: the top-left tile, the top-right tile and the bottom-left tile. Each bank is a dark rectangular frame holding three round sockets in a vertical column; a socket is either lit, drawn as a filled amber disc, or empty, drawn as a pale disc. A bank's count is simply how many of its three sockets are lit, and it never starts above two. The fourth tile, at the bottom right, is the tick patch: a dark frame holding twelve small square slots in three rows of four, of which some are filled solid teal and the rest are pale. Each teal slot is one tick, and the ticks are applied one after another. Applying one tick works like this: the bottom-left bank gains one lit lamp; but if that bank already shows two lit lamps it instead empties to zero lit lamps and one tick is passed to the top-right bank, which gains one lit lamp under the same rule and, if it already shows two, empties to zero and passes one tick to the top-left bank, which likewise gains one lit lamp and empties to zero if it already shows two. Exactly one bank is marked by a thin red rectangle drawn just inside its dark frame. The meter may sit anywhere on the canvas, and the sockets that happen to be lit within a bank carry no meaning beyond their number. After every tick in the patch has been applied, how many lamps are lit in the bank marked by the red rectangle? Answer with one of zero, one or two.
